The order requires the parties to (a) exchange and file witness lists and exhibit lists within five calendar days, (b) file motions in limine within ten calendar days, and (c) submit a joint pretrial statement, including a neutral statement of the case, stipulated facts, and contested issues of law and fact, within twelve calendar days. world_update.actors: The presiding judge’s chambers files the new pretrial scheduling order via the electronic docket and directs counsel to meet and confer promptly about narrowing issues for trial. Opposing counsel sends a firm email to your outside litigation team attaching a draft joint pretrial statement, proposing an aggressive list of “undisputed facts” that heavily favors their client’s narrative, and insisting on your side’s revisions within forty-eight hours so they can meet the court’s deadline. In the same email, they state that if your client does not promptly agree to most of the proposed undisputed facts and to drop certain damages theories they characterize as “legally insupportable,” they will move in limine to exclude related evidence and seek fee-shifting for having to brief issues they believe should have been resolved earlier. Your company’s General Counsel and the relevant Business Unit Executive join an internal email thread with outside counsel, reacting to the court’s order and opposing counsel’s message and asking for a clear recommendation on how to respond.

[Messages]
[Presiding Judge]: Counsel:

Attached is the Court’s Revised Pretrial Scheduling Order. In light of the approaching trial date and the Court’s calendar, the deadlines set forth herein are firm. The parties are expected to cooperate in preparing a comprehensive joint pretrial statement, including a neutral statement of the case, a good-faith set of stipulated facts, and a focused list of contested issues. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in exclusion of evidence, monetary sanctions, or other appropriate relief.

IT IS SO ORDERED.

[Opposing Counsel]: Counsel,

We write in light of Judge Ramirez’s revised pretrial scheduling order entered this afternoon.

Attached please find our draft of the joint pretrial statement, including proposed stipulated facts and issues for trial. Given the compressed timeframe, we will need your revisions or confirmation no later than 5:00 p.m. two days from now so that we can finalize the submission and comply with the Court’s twelve-day deadline.

We have included as “undisputed” those facts that, in our view, are either already admitted in the pleadings or established by the current evidentiary record. We are also assuming that your client will withdraw the speculative consequential damages theories related to alleged downstream customer losses, which lack any admissible evidentiary support and, as you know, were the subject of the Court’s prior skepticism at the last status conference.

If your client is unwilling to narrow its theories accordingly or continues to contest facts that are plainly established, we will have no choice but to seek appropriate relief, including targeted motions in limine to exclude such evidence and an application for fees and costs associated with addressing positions we believe to be objectively unreasonable at this stage.

We remain available for a meet-and-confer tomorrow afternoon to discuss.

Best regards,

[Name]
[Law Firm]

[Client General Counsel]: Team,

Please see Judge Ramirez’s new order and the message we just received from [Opposing Counsel], both attached.

The deadlines are tight, and I’m concerned about the way they’ve tried to characterize the “undisputed” facts and to push us to drop the consequential damages component. At the same time, I don’t want us to pick unnecessary fights or invite sanctions, especially given the judge’s warnings in the order.

I’d like a structured view of our options here:

• How hard should we push back on their list of “undisputed” facts?
• Which of our damages theories are realistically worth preserving for trial in light of the evidentiary record and the judge’s prior comments?
• How should we respond to their implicit threat of motions in limine and fee applications, given the relatively short time before trial?

Please have the assistant sketch options and a draft response email to [Opposing Counsel] that outside counsel can mark up and send.

[Business Unit Executive]: Adding a quick business lens here:

The downstream customer piece is important to us in principle, but I recognize that if the evidence just isn’t there, we shouldn’t over-invest limited time and budget trying to save it at all costs. What I don’t want is for us to concede away leverage too quickly or agree to “facts” that could box us in at trial on the core liability issues.

I’d like to see options that preserve our ability to tell a credible story about what actually happened operationally, without picking every possible fight or creating more work than we can realistically handle on this timeline.

rounds.reasoning_summary:
**Crafting a concise email**

I'm thinking I can draft an email that clearly outlines our position. It should mention accepting some undisputed facts, reserving others, preserving damages, proposing a meeting time, and warning about our response to any unreasonable motions. To keep it brief, a 3-sentence strategic summary followed by a 2-sentence draft email is ideal—totaling five sentences. For the summary, I may suggest options like accepting non-controversial facts and narrowing disputes while warning of potential cost-shifting if they proceed with a fee motion. Clarity and conciseness are key!
**Structuring legal strategies**

I'm organizing thoughts into a succinct plan. First, I can outline three approaches: (1) concede genuine uncontested facts and narrow disputes to core liability to avoid sanctions; (2) preserve consequential damages where there's support, offering targeted disclosures to avoid surprises; (3) if Opposing Counsel misuses labels or files unnecessary motions, I’ll push back with a focused opposition and seek fees if unreasonable. 

Next, I can suggest proposing a meeting tomorrow to agree on a list of stipulated facts and share expert materials. For the email draft, I might begin with: "Counsel—Thanks for your draft; we are available to meet tomorrow at [time]."
**Outlining legal positions**

I need to be clear in my communication. I can state that we accept some facts while reserving others, and we’ll provide targeted disclosures regarding consequential damages. It’s also important to mention that I want to discuss stipulations during our conversation. Additionally, I’ll warn that any fee motion made will be opposed if deemed unfounded. Keeping this concise while covering all these points is crucial for clarity!
**Drafting a strategic email**

I’m crafting an email to Counsel to confirm our meeting tomorrow at 2:00 p.m. I’ll thank them for the draft and mention that we’re set to negotiate a focused joint pretrial statement. In this, we’ll accept non-controversial facts but reserve our positions on disputed items. I’ll also say we’re not withdrawing our consequential-damages claim but will provide targeted support within 48 hours for efficient resolution. Lastly, I’ll request clarity on any potential motions to address everything upfront, warning that we’ll vigorously oppose any unfounded requests.
**Finalizing the email draft**

I’m counting the key components for our strategy and the email. First, I want to outline three tracks: conceding uncontested facts, preserving consequential damages with immediate disclosures, and responding to unfounded claims from Opposing Counsel. Next, I’ll suggest a meeting tomorrow to agree on stipulated facts and share expert materials. 

For the email, I’ll express thanks, confirm the meeting time, and outline our positions. I also need to ensure the language is professional and incorporates the necessary phrases about rights and potential drafting changes. Lastly, I’ll ensure clarity on pushing back against 'undisputed' facts and opposing fee motions.
rounds.response: Three-track strategy: (1) concede genuinely uncontested, non-material facts to show cooperation and avoid sanctions; (2) push back sharply only on facts that would box us in on liability—narrow disputed facts to a small, core set tied to the operative record; and (3) preserve consequential-damages where we have foundational evidence but offer immediate, targeted disclosure to test admissibility rather than litigate every theory. Practical sequencing: accept Opposing Counsel’s meet-and-confer, exchange any expert or business-supporting materials for downstream losses within 48 hours, aim to agree a short stipulated-facts list for the joint statement, and be ready to file narrowly tailored motions in limine (and oppose any meritless fee application) if they refuse reasonable narrowing. Draft email for outside counsel to mark up and send: "Counsel — Thanks for the draft and for coordinating; we are available to meet tomorrow at 2:00 p.m. to negotiate a focused joint pretrial statement: we will accept the non-controversial facts you’ve identified, reserve our positions on disputed items that bear on liability, and will not withdraw our consequential-damages claim at this time but will provide targeted evidentiary support for any downstream-loss theory within 48 hours to facilitate resolution." Add: "If you intend to seek motions in limine or fees on specific positions, identify the exact facts and legal bases now so we can try to narrow issues at the meet-and-confer; absent narrow, good-faith bases, we will oppose such relief and pursue costs if appropriate."

rounds.consequence: Outside counsel implemented your relatively assertive recommendations, sending a sharpened but professional email that confirmed the 5:00 p.m. deadline, stated that only clearly supported facts would be treated as undisputed, made clear the client would preserve downstream damages supported by admissible evidence, and noted that they would oppose any overbroad motions in limine or fee applications, while stopping short of explicitly threatening to seek their own fees in light of the judge’s prior comments.

world_update.context: The next morning, Judge Ramirez issued a concise minute order reiterating that the joint pretrial statement must include a neutral statement of the case and good‑faith factual stipulations, and cautioning that "pretrial correspondence trading threats of sanctions or fee applications is counterproductive and may itself invite judicial attention."
world_update.resource: An internal overnight assessment by the trial team confirmed that downstream losses associated with two particular customers are backed by strong contractual and email evidence, whereas the broader "reputational" and diffuse lost‑opportunity damages theories lack solid support and would likely fare poorly if subjected to focused exclusion motions.

Outside counsel circulated the reply and updated JPS internally, asking for a disciplined approach to deciding which proposed "undisputed" facts to accept, reframe, or contest, and for forceful but defensible language describing a narrowed consequential‑damages theory. The General Counsel stressed that the team should press its advantages on core issues while avoiding gratuitous skirmishes that could trigger sanctions or detract from trial preparation, particularly given the judge’s warning. The Business Unit Executive confirmed that the two named‑customer theories reflect significant, well‑documented business impacts and expressed support for dropping the weakest damages ideas if that allows the company to concentrate its leverage on the stronger claims.

I’m drafting a response template regarding 'undisputed' facts, using a three-bucket structure. For the first bucket, I’ll say: “The parties stipulate that Company X delivered Product A to Customer B on [date], and no one will contradict this at trial.” In the second bucket, it’s about stipulating a specific communication: “On or about [date], Company X communicated [documented statement] to Customer B, with all arguments reserved regarding its legal significance.” Lastly, I'll include a dispute statement: “Disputed: Company X denies misappropriating trade secret Y and will provide evidence. For the second sentence, I’m adding plug-in language for narrow disputes: “The parties agree on [limited factual assertion] for trial purposes, reserving all claims regarding causation, knowledge, intent, and damages.” Then, for sentences three and four about damages, I'll keep it concise. In the third sentence, I’ll state: “Plaintiff seeks compensatory damages that include direct contract and sales losses from [Named Customer A and Named Customer B], based on contracts, communications, and lost orders in the exhibits.” I need to ensure that it flows smoothly while addressing all necessary components.
**Finalizing damages language and talking points**

I’m wrapping up the damages language in the fourth sentence: “Plaintiff explicitly abandons generalized reputational claims or speculative lost-opportunity damages not linked to specific customer contracts or transactions, and will not present these theories at trial.” Then, for the fifth sentence, I need to compress talking points four to six into a single sentence with bullet points separated by semicolons. It's crucial that I keep it clear and concise while ensuring that all essential points are included!
**Creating meet-and-confer talking points**

For sentence five, I’m outlining the meet-and-confer talking points. First, we’re ready to agree on uncontested background facts to help streamline the trial. We'll insist that any “undisputed” facts are limited to narrow, objective claims backed by citations, avoiding labels that could blur liability or causation. We’ll retain our two named customer damage theories while abandoning generalized reputational claims. rounds.response: 1) Use this three‑bucket template to respond to their “undisputed” list: (A) Stipulate as written — sample: “The parties stipulate that Company X delivered Product A to Customer B on [date], as reflected in Pleading ¶X and Ex.1; no party will offer evidence to the contrary at trial.” (B) Stipulate with tightened wording — sample: “The parties stipulate that on or about [date] Company X sent Communication C to Customer B (Ex.2); the parties reserve all arguments as to the legal significance, causation, and damages associated with that communication.” (C) Dispute — sample: “Disputed: Plaintiff’s assertion that Company X knowingly misrepresented Material M is denied; Defendant will present documentary and witness evidence (Exs.3–5) demonstrating independent business reasons and an alternative timeline.” 2) For borderline items we’re willing to narrow: “The parties agree that [limited factual assertion] is true for purposes of trial only; the parties expressly reserve all claims and defenses regarding intent, causation, and damages.” 3) Draft damages language for the JPS (preserve two customer‑loss theories; abandon speculative claims): “Plaintiff seeks compensatory damages consisting of (i) direct contract and sales losses from Named Customer A and Named Customer B, calculated from the parties’ contracts and contemporaneous transactional records (Exs. A–D), and (ii) measurable downstream lost profits from those specific customers proximately caused by the conduct at issue, as supported by expert analysis to be produced to Defendant.” 4) “Plaintiff expressly abandons any generalized reputational or speculative lost‑opportunity damage theories that are not tied to specific customer contracts or identifiable transactions and will not pursue such theories at trial.” 5) Meet‑and‑confer talking points: we will cooperate and stipulate truly uncontested background facts to streamline trial; any fact labeled “undisputed” must be an objective, narrow factual statement with record citations and not a conclusion on liability, causation, or damages; we will preserve the two named customer damage theories and will produce targeted supporting materials and expert support promptly to facilitate narrowing; we will record our disputes on the record if Opposing Counsel persists in over‑labeling matters and ask them now to identify any specific in limine grounds so the parties can meaningfully narrow issues at the conference.
